expectedText:
HIRING AN UNLICENSED CONTRACTOR — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Construction Services, Inc.

ABOUT THIS HIRING AN UNLICENSED CONTRACTOR INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's contractor's license requirement for work covered by Chapter 9 (commencing with Section 7000) of Division 3 of the Business and Professions Code, the rebuttable presumption of employee status that Labor Code Section 2750.5 attaches to unlicensed persons performing such work, and the consequences that follow from proceeding without the required license, including criminal penalties, loss of the right to sue for compensation, and a narrow dollar-threshold exemption for casual or minor work. Acme Construction Services, Inc. has described its use of, or engagement with, contractors performing work that may require a California contractor's license as follows: We hire subcontractors for electrical and plumbing work on renovation projects. This document states the content of the statutes and of published case law; it does not determine whether any particular worker, task, or project falls within the statutory definition of a "contractor" or within the scope of Chapter 9, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice or for consulting a licensed attorney.

ACTING AS A CONTRACTOR WITHOUT A LICENSE IS A CRIME
Unless a statutory exemption applies, it is a misdemeanor under California law for a person to engage in the business of, or act in the capacity of, a contractor within California without being licensed in accordance with Chapter 9 (commencing with Section 7000) of Division 3 of the Business and Professions Code.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Unless exempted from this chapter, it is a misdemeanor for a person to engage in the business of, or act in the capacity of, a contractor within this state under either of the following conditions:"
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7028(a), Bus. & Prof. Code § 7028(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7028.)
  "The person is not licensed in accordance with this chapter."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7028(a)(1), Bus. & Prof. Code § 7028(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7028.)
  Known gap: This clause states the general rule and its unlicensed-status branch only; Section 7028(a)(2) separately makes it a misdemeanor to perform licensed work under a license currently suspended for failure to pay a civil penalty, comply with a correction order, or resolve outstanding final liabilities, which is not restated here. Numerous express statutory exemptions from Chapter 9's licensing requirement exist (Sections 7040 et seq.), including the small-job exemption addressed in a separate clause of this document; this clause does not catalog those exemptions.

ESCALATING CRIMINAL PENALTIES FOR REPEAT UNLICENSED CONTRACTING
A first conviction for acting as an unlicensed contractor in violation of Section 7028 is punishable by a fine not exceeding $5,000, by imprisonment in a county jail not exceeding six months, or by both. A third or subsequent conviction is punishable by a fine of not less than $5,000, up to the greater of $10,000 or 20 percent of the contract price or aggregate payments received, and by imprisonment in a county jail for not more than one year or less than 90 days.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "A first conviction for the offense described in this section is punishable by a fine not exceeding five thousand dollars ($5,000) or by imprisonment in a county jail not exceeding six months, or by both that fine and imprisonment."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7028(b), Bus. & Prof. Code § 7028(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7028.)
  "A third or subsequent conviction for the offense described in this section is punishable by a fine of not less than five thousand dollars ($5,000) nor more than the greater amount of ten thousand dollars ($10,000) or 20 percent of the contract price, or 20 percent of the aggregate payments made to, or at the direction of, the unlicensed person, and by imprisonment in a county jail for not more than one year or less than 90 days."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7028(d), Bus. & Prof. Code § 7028(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7028.)
  Known gap: The penalty for a second conviction, stated in Section 7028(c), falls between the first- and third-conviction penalties quoted here and is not separately quoted in this clause; it generally imposes a fine equal to the greater of $5,000 or 20 percent of the contract price or aggregate payments, together with a minimum 90-day county jail term, subject to a court's discretion to impose a lesser sentence in an unusual case. Section 7028(f) separately defines "the contract price" for a person who furnished materials and labor on an hourly basis, which is not restated here.

RESTITUTION RIGHTS FOR A PERSON WHO USED AN UNLICENSED CONTRACTOR'S SERVICES
Upon a conviction under Section 7028, a person who used the services of the unlicensed person is treated as a victim of crime and is eligible for restitution for economic losses under Penal Code Section 1202.4(f), regardless of whether that person knew the contractor was unlicensed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "For any conviction under this section, a person who utilized the services of the unlicensed person is a victim of crime and is eligible, pursuant to subdivision (f) of Section 1202.4 of the Penal Code, for restitution for economic losses, regardless of whether he or she had knowledge that the person was unlicensed."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7028(h), Bus. & Prof. Code § 7028(h) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7028.)
  Known gap: This clause does not describe the restitution procedure under Penal Code Section 1202.4(f) itself, such as how economic losses are calculated or claimed in the criminal proceeding.

PRESUMPTION THAT AN UNLICENSED WORKER PERFORMING LICENSED WORK IS AN EMPLOYEE
Under Labor Code Section 2750.5, there is a rebuttable presumption, affecting the burden of proof, that a worker performing services for which a contractor's license is required under Chapter 9 (commencing with Section 7000) of Division 3 of the Business and Professions Code — or who performs such services for a person who is required to hold such a license — is an employee rather than an independent contractor.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "There is a rebuttable presumption affecting the burden of proof that a worker performing services for which a license is required pursuant to Chapter 9 (commencing with Section 7000) of Division 3 of the Business and Professions Code, or who is performing such services for a person who is required to obtain such a license is an employee rather than an independent contractor."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2750.5, Lab. Code § 2750.5 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2750.5)
  Known gap: This clause states the presumption itself; the factors by which independent contractor status may be proven despite the presumption, and the additional licensure condition that applies on top of those factors, are addressed in separate clauses of this document.

FACTORS BEARING ON INDEPENDENT CONTRACTOR STATUS DESPITE THE PRESUMPTION
Labor Code Section 2750.5 states that proof of independent contractor status includes satisfactory proof that the individual has the right to control and discretion as to the manner of performance, with the result of the work rather than the means of accomplishing it being the primary factor bargained for; that the individual is customarily engaged in an independently established business; and that the individual's independent contractor status is bona fide and not a subterfuge to avoid employee status.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "That the individual has the right to control and discretion as to the manner of performance of the contract for services in that the result of the work and not the means by which it is accomplished is the primary factor bargained for."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2750.5(a), Lab. Code § 2750.5(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2750.5)
  "That the individual is customarily engaged in an independently established business."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2750.5(b), Lab. Code § 2750.5(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2750.5)
  "That the individual’s independent contractor status is bona fide and not a subterfuge to avoid employee status."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2750.5(c), Lab. Code § 2750.5(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2750.5)
  Known gap: Following subdivisions (a) through (c), Section 2750.5 lists additional cumulative factors evidencing bona fide independent contractor status in a separate, unlettered paragraph — not as part of subdivision (c) itself — including substantial business investment, holding out as self-employed, project-based compensation, control over time and place of work, supplying one's own tools, hiring employees, performing work outside the principal's ordinary course of business, performing work requiring a particular skill, holding a Business and Professions Code license, the parties' intent, and whether the relationship is terminable at will — which are not separately quoted in this clause.

A VALID CONTRACTOR'S LICENSE IS A CONDITION OF INDEPENDENT CONTRACTOR STATUS
Labor Code Section 2750.5 provides that, in addition to the factors otherwise bearing on independent contractor status, any person performing a function or activity for which a contractor's license is required under Chapter 9 (commencing with Section 7000) of Division 3 of the Business and Professions Code must hold a valid contractor's license as a condition of having independent contractor status.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "In addition to the factors contained in subdivisions (a), (b), and (c), any person performing any function or activity for which a license is required pursuant to Chapter 9 (commencing with Section 7000) of Division 3 of the Business and Professions Code shall hold a valid contractors’ license as a condition of having independent contractor status."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2750.5, Lab. Code § 2750.5 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2750.5)
  Known gap: No specific gap was recorded for this clause when it was verified; the citation quotes were checked verbatim against the fetched source text, but no narrower limitation was noted.

RELATIONSHIP OF THE PRESUMPTION TO WORKERS' COMPENSATION COVERAGE
Labor Code Section 2750.5 states that, for purposes of workers' compensation law, the presumption it creates is a supplement to the existing statutory definitions of employee and independent contractor and is not intended to lessen the coverage of employees under Divisions 4 and 5 of the Labor Code.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "For purposes of workers’ compensation law, this presumption is a supplement to the existing statutory definitions of employee and independent contractor, and is not intended to lessen the coverage of employees under Division 4 and Division 5."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 2750.5, Lab. Code § 2750.5 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2750.5)
  Known gap: This clause does not restate the workers' compensation coverage provisions of Labor Code Divisions 4 and 5 that Section 2750.5 refers to.

AN UNLICENSED CONTRACTOR CANNOT SUE FOR COMPENSATION, AND THE HIRING PARTY MAY RECOVER AMOUNTS PAID
Under Business and Professions Code Section 7031(a), except as provided in subdivision (e), a person engaged in the business of or acting as a contractor may not bring or maintain any action to recover compensation for work requiring a license under Chapter 9 without alleging that they were a duly licensed contractor at all times during performance, regardless of the merits of the underlying claim. Under Section 7031(b), except as provided in subdivision (e), a person who used the services of an unlicensed contractor may bring an action to recover all compensation paid to that unlicensed contractor for the work performed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "no person engaged in the business or acting in the capacity of a contractor, may bring or maintain any action, or recover in law or equity in any action, in any court of this state for the collection of compensation for the performance of any act or contract where a license is required by this chapter without alleging that they were a duly licensed contractor at all times during the performance of that act or contract regardless of the merits of the cause of action brought by the person"
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7031(a), Bus. & Prof. Code § 7031(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7031.)
  "a person who utilizes the services of an unlicensed contractor may bring an action in any court of competent jurisdiction in this state to recover all compensation paid to the unlicensed contractor for performance of any act or contract."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7031(b), Bus. & Prof. Code § 7031(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7031.)
  Known gap: This clause states the general bar and recovery right of Section 7031(a)-(b) only. Subdivision (a) contains an exception, not restated here, for contractors who are each individually licensed but fail to comply with Section 7029 (the joint-venture licensing provision). Subdivision (e) creates a limited, evidentiary-hearing-dependent judicial-doctrine-of-substantial-compliance exception to subdivision (a) for a person who was duly licensed before the work but let licensure lapse, which does not apply to a person who was never licensed in California; that exception is not restated in this clause. Subdivision (d) separately addresses how licensure is proven when controverted, and subdivision (c) separately voids certain security interests taken to secure payment for unlicensed work; neither is restated here.

THE CALIFORNIA SUPREME COURT ON THE PURPOSE OF STRICT LICENSE-FORFEITURE ENFORCEMENT
The California Supreme Court has stated that the purpose of California's contractor licensing law is to protect the public from incompetence and dishonesty in those who provide building and construction services, and that Business and Professions Code Section 7031 advances this purpose by withholding judicial aid from those who seek compensation for unlicensed contract work. The Court has further described it as settled that Section 7031 applies even where its application works an injustice on the unlicensed contractor, quoting the rule that Section 7031 represents a legislative determination that the importance of deterring unlicensed persons from engaging in the contracting business outweighs any harshness between the parties, and that such deterrence can best be realized by denying violators the right to maintain any action for compensation in the courts of the state.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "The purpose of the licensing law is to protect the public from incompetence and dishonesty in those who provide building and construction services."
  — Hydrotech Systems, Ltd. v. Oasis Waterpark, 52 Cal. 3d 988, 997 (1991) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1131503/hydrotech-systems-ltd-v-oasis-waterpark/)
  "Section 7031 advances this purpose by withholding judicial aid from those who seek compensation for unlicensed contract work."
  — Hydrotech Systems, Ltd. v. Oasis Waterpark, 52 Cal. 3d 988, 997 (1991) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1131503/hydrotech-systems-ltd-v-oasis-waterpark/)
  "Section 7031 represents a legislative determination that the importance of deterring unlicensed persons from engaging in the contracting business outweighs any harshness between the parties, and that such deterrence can best be realized by denying violators the right to maintain any action for compensation in the courts of this state."
  — Hydrotech Systems, Ltd. v. Oasis Waterpark, 52 Cal. 3d 988, 997 (1991) (quoting Lewis & Queen v. N.M. Ball Sons, 48 Cal. 2d 141, 151 (1957)) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1131503/hydrotech-systems-ltd-v-oasis-waterpark/)
  Known gap: This clause quotes the California Supreme Court's statement of Section 7031's purpose and its description of the settled rule that the statute applies even where enforcement produces a harsh result for the unlicensed contractor; it does not restate the specific holding of Hydrotech itself, which concerned whether an out-of-state contractor performing an isolated transaction in California could invoke a judicially created exception, a question the Court answered by looking to whether the Legislature's 1989 amendments to Section 7031 displaced any such exception — a separate analysis not summarized in this clause.

CASUAL, MINOR WORK UNDER $1,000 IS EXEMPT FROM THE LICENSING CHAPTER
Business and Professions Code Section 7048(a) exempts from the licensing chapter a work or operation on one undertaking or project where the aggregate contract price for labor, materials, and all other items is less than $1,000, provided the work is of a casual, minor, or inconsequential nature and does not require a building permit. Under Section 7048(c), this exemption does not apply to a person who advertises or otherwise holds themselves out to the public as a contractor, or who employs another person to perform or assist in performing the work.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "This chapter does not apply to a work or operation on one undertaking or project by one or more contracts if the aggregate contract price for labor, materials, and all other items is less than one thousand dollars ($1,000), that work or operation being considered of casual, minor, or inconsequential nature, and the work or operation does not require a building permit."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7048(a), Bus. & Prof. Code § 7048(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7048.)
  "This section does not apply to a person who does either of the following:"
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7048(c), Bus. & Prof. Code § 7048(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7048.)
  "Advertises or puts out a sign or card or other device that might indicate to the public that the person is a contractor or that the person is qualified to engage in the business of a contractor."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7048(c)(1), Bus. & Prof. Code § 7048(c)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7048.)
  "Employs another person to perform, or assist in performing, the work or operation."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 7048(c)(2), Bus. & Prof. Code § 7048(c)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=7048.)
  Known gap: Section 7048(b) separately provides that this exemption does not apply where construction work is only part of a larger or major operation, or where a project is divided into sub-$1,000 contracts to evade the licensing chapter, which is not restated in this clause. This exemption applies only to the licensing requirement of Chapter 9 generally; it does not itself alter the Section 2750.5 employee-status presumption addressed elsewhere in this document, which by its own terms applies where a license "is required." The $1,000 threshold reflected here took effect January 1, 2026, under a 2025 amendment; the threshold was previously $500.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
This information sheet regarding California's contractor licensing requirement, Business and Professions Code Sections 7028, 7031, and 7048, and Labor Code Section 2750.5, was prepared by Jordan T. Reyes for Acme Construction Services, Inc. and reviewed in Sacramento, California on September 10, 2026. It reflects the statutory and case-law text as of the date checked above and does not reflect any amendments or decisions issued after that date, and it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney.

citations.quote: This chapter does not apply to a work or operation on one undertaking or project by one or more contracts if the aggregate contract price for labor, materials, and all other items is less than one thousand dollars ($1,000), that work or operation being considered of casual, minor, or inconsequential nature, and the work or operation does not require a building permit.
This section does not apply to a person who does either of the following:
Advertises or puts out a sign or card or other device that might indicate to the public that the person is a contractor or that the person is qualified to engage in the business of a contractor.
Employs another person to perform, or assist in performing, the work or operation.

expectedJSON.gap: Section 7048(b) separately provides that this exemption does not apply where construction work is only part of a larger or major operation, or where a project is divided into sub-$1,000 contracts to evade the licensing chapter, which is not restated in this clause. This exemption applies only to the licensing requirement of Chapter 9 generally; it does not itself alter the Section 2750.5 employee-status presumption addressed elsewhere in this document, which by its own terms applies where a license "is required." The $1,000 threshold reflected here took effect January 1, 2026, under a 2025 amendment; the threshold was previously $500.

expectedJSON.body: This information sheet regarding California's contractor licensing requirement, Business and Professions Code Sections 7028, 7031, and 7048, and Labor Code Section 2750.5, was prepared by Jordan T. Reyes for Acme Construction Services, Inc. and reviewed in Sacramento, California on September 10, 2026. It reflects the statutory and case-law text as of the date checked above and does not reflect any amendments or decisions issued after that date, and it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney.
